Small Models That Fit a 6 GB RTX 2060

Sep 5, 2026 · 7 min read · Guide

Six gigabytes of VRAM sounds tight in 2026, but it is enough for real writing and agent work if you pick the right quantization and leave heavy reasoning off the GPU. This is the setup we use daily on an RTX 2060 with 32 GB of system RAM: drafting, QA and summarisation all run locally, and cloud models are called only when a draft is truly stuck.

The VRAM math

A 7-billion-parameter model at 16-bit needs about 14 GB. Quantize it to 4-bit and it drops to ~4.2 GB, leaving headroom for context and KV cache. The trick is the format: Q4_K_M is the sweet spot for quality versus size, Q5_K_M buys a little clarity for 15% more VRAM, and Q4_0 is faster but duller on nuanced tasks. For this site, qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M (~4.4 GB) and mistral:7b-instruct-q4_K_M (~4.1 GB) are the daily drivers. Both fit fully on the GPU with a 4096-token context and still leave ~800 MB free for overhead.

What fits comfortably

  • 7–8B Q4: Fully on GPU, 35–55 tokens/sec with llama.cpp or ollama. Ideal for drafting, rewriting, HTML fixes and weekly notes.
  • Phi-3 Mini 3.8B Q4: ~2.3 GB, absurdly fast (70+ t/s), perfect for summarisation and quick QA checks. Slightly weaker on long-form coherence.
  • Gemma 2 9B Q4: ~5.4 GB with 2K context — fits, but keep the prompt short or clip context to 2048. Better style than 7B models for essays.
  • Embeddings + rerank: nomic-embed-text (~0.5 GB) and a tiny reranker stay resident on the GPU. They are small, hot and called constantly for search, so never offload them.

What needs offload

A 13–14B Q4 model is ~8–8.5 GB even quantized, so it will not fit fully. With llama.cpp you can split layers: keep ~30 layers on GPU and spill the rest to CPU RAM.

# full offload for 7B — fast
ollama run qwen2.5:7b-instruct-q4_K_M

# partial offload for 13B — slower but usable
./llama-cli -m yi-34b-q4_k_m.gguf --gpu-layers 32 --ctx-size 4096

Expect 8–15 t/s with partial offload on a 4-core i5 — fine for a nightly polish pass, painful for interactive chat. Our rule: if interactive speed falls below 20 t/s, the model is too big for the task. Swap it.

Our daily stack

ollama run qwen2.5:7b        # drafting blog posts
ollama run phi3:mini         # quick summaries, titles
ollama run nomic-embed-text  # local search over posts
opencode --model qwen2.5:7b  # agent runtime, no cloud key

We keep one model resident at a time. Loading and unloading costs seconds, not minutes, and avoids VRAM fragmentation. Context is capped at 4096 for 7B and 2048 for 9B+ models. Temperature 0.6 for drafts, 0.2 for edits — higher creativity early, lower drift when fixing facts.

Three tips from real runs

1. Pin VRAM, watch the cache. Use nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 1 while prompting. If memory.used spikes above 5.8 GB, shorten context or switch to Q4_0. The KV cache grows with context length, not parameter count, and is the usual OOM culprit.

2. Keep the prompt scaffold small. Our agent prompts are under 600 tokens: role, goal, constraints, workspace layout. Long system prompts eat cache and slow every inference. Put checklists in files, not in the prompt.

3. Measure, don't guess. We logged tokens/sec and quality for a week. 7B Q4_K_M drafts were indistinguishable from cloud 70B for short blog posts in blind edits, but cloud won on complex research synthesis. Now local handles 80% of posts; cloud is the escalator, not the engine.

An RTX 2060 will not train a frontier model, but it will run a full editorial loop — draft, review, publish — without a subscription. Start with a good 7B Q4, keep embeddings on the card, and treat 13B+ as a sometimes tool, not a default. Your power bill and your latency will thank you.
